Not quite. D is the final product. It isn't a reactant in the slow step, so it doesn't appear in the rate law. Making more D doesn't speed anything up.
Correct. The slow step, A + B → C, controls the speed. It's an elementary step with one A and one B colliding, so each is first order: rate = k[A][B].

p: Many reactions happen in a series of small steps called a mechanism. The slowest step limits the overall speed, like the narrowest part of a road. It's called the rate-determining step.

For an elementary step, the rate law comes straight from the step: each reactant's exponent equals its coefficient in that step. When the slow step is the first step, its rate law is the overall rate law.
Two things never show up in the final rate law: species that only react after the slow step, and intermediates, which are made in one step and used up in another.

Not quite. The temperature rise is right. But exothermic means the system gives off heat, so ΔH, which is measured from the system's point of view, is negative, not positive.
Correct. An exothermic reaction releases heat. That heat flows into the calorimeter's contents, so their temperature goes up. The system lost energy, so ΔH is negative.
Not quite. Energy is conserved, but it doesn't stay put. It moves from the reaction into the surroundings as heat, and that's exactly what makes the thermometer reading go up.

p: The system is the reaction you're studying. The surroundings are everything else, like the water in a calorimeter and the thermometer in it. ΔH, the enthalpy change, is the heat the system gives off or takes in at constant pressure, always measured from the system's point of view.
Exothermic: the system releases heat, so ΔH is negative, and the surroundings get warmer. Endothermic: the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive, and the surroundings get colder.
A calorimeter measures the surroundings' temperature. So a temperature rise tells you the reaction was exothermic.

Endothermic: ΔH > 0, surroundings cool down
ΔH is from the system's point of view

ox: Correct. The transition state is the highest point on the energy curve for a step. It's an in-between arrangement that exists for only an instant, so it can't be isolated.
Not quite. A low point between two peaks is an intermediate, a real species with some stability that can sometimes be detected or isolated. The transition state is a peak, not a valley.
Not quite. The products' energy is the level where the curve ends on the right side of the diagram. It's an end point, not the peak along the way.
Not quite. The energy difference between reactants and products is ΔG or ΔH, a single number, not a species or a point on the curve. The transition state is a specific spot: the top of the hill.

p: A reaction coordinate diagram plots energy (up the side) as a reaction moves from reactants to products (along the bottom). The curve rises over one or more hills before settling at the products.

The top of each hill is a transition state, the fleeting arrangement of atoms partway through a change. The height from the reactants up to that peak is the activation energy. Transition states can't be isolated.

A valley between two hills is an intermediate. It's a real species that sticks around briefly, so it can sometimes be detected or isolated. More steps means more hills, and an intermediate between each pair.

mem: Transition state: the peak, can't be isolated
Intermediate: a valley, can sometimes be isolated
Activation energy: from reactants up to the peak
d_5E_17.trap: Swapping peaks and valleys. Peak is the transition state; valley is the intermediate.
d_5E_17.plain: Roll a ball over a hill. The ball can't sit balanced on the very top; that's the transition state. A dip partway along where it can rest for a moment is the intermediate.

fig.cap: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, spontaneity flips at T = ΔH/ΔS.
fig.alt: ΔG of protein folding against temperature, crossing zero at 400 K.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Question data.

ox: Not quite. To be spontaneous at every temperature, both terms must help: a negative ΔH and a positive ΔS (so −TΔS is negative too). Here ΔS is negative, so −TΔS is a positive term that grows with T and eventually wins.
Not quite. Spontaneous only at high temperature goes with positive ΔH and positive ΔS: the TΔS term needs high T to overcome an uphill ΔH. This choice flips the signs of the case in the question.
Not quite. Never spontaneous needs both terms to hurt: positive ΔH and negative ΔS. Here ΔH is negative, which helps, so at low enough temperature the reaction does go.

Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. ΔH is negative (helps). ΔS is negative, so −TΔS is positive (hurts). At low T the hurting term is small, so ΔG stays negative. At high T, −TΔS becomes a big positive number and ΔG turns positive.

concept.t: How the signs of ΔH and ΔS set spontaneity
p: ΔG tells you whether a reaction is spontaneous, meaning it happens on its own: negative ΔG means yes. The equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS has two parts. A negative ΔH (giving off heat) helps. A positive ΔS (more disorder) helps, because it makes −TΔS negative.
If both parts help (ΔH negative, ΔS positive), it's spontaneous at all temperatures. If both hurt (ΔH positive, ΔS negative), it's never spontaneous.

If they disagree, temperature decides, because T multiplies only the entropy term. Both negative: ΔH wins when it's cold, so spontaneous at low T. Both positive: TΔS wins when it's hot, so spontaneous at high T.

mem: ΔH −, ΔS +: always spontaneous
ΔH +, ΔS −: never spontaneous
Both negative: spontaneous at low T
Both positive: spontaneous at high T
d_5E_20.sc: When the signs match, temperature picks the winner. Low T shrinks the TΔS term so ΔH wins; high T makes TΔS win.
d_5E_20.trap: Mixing up which matching-sign case goes with low T and which goes with high T.
d_5E_20.plain: Think of water freezing into ice: it gives off heat and gets more ordered. That only happens when it's cold. Warm it up and the ice falls apart.

ox: Not quite. A positive ΔG goes with Q greater than K, when there's too much product and the reaction runs in reverse. Here Q is less than K. This choice also pairs a positive ΔG with a forward reaction, which don't go together.
Not quite. A negative ΔG means the forward direction is favored, so 'negative ΔG' and 'runs in reverse' contradict each other. Q < K points forward.
Correct. ΔG = RT ln(Q/K). With Q less than K, Q/K is below 1, so its natural log is negative. RT is positive, so ΔG is negative. The reaction moves forward, making products until Q rises to equal K.
Not quite. ΔG = 0 only at equilibrium, when Q = K. Here Q is less than K, so the system isn't at equilibrium yet and still has somewhere to go.

p: K is the ratio of products to reactants once a reaction has settled at equilibrium. Q is the same ratio calculated from whatever mixture you have right now. Comparing the two tells you which way the reaction has to move.

If Q is less than K, there's not enough product yet, so the reaction runs forward. If Q is greater than K, there's too much product, so it runs in reverse. If Q equals K, it's at equilibrium and nothing changes overall.
ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) puts this in energy terms: Q < K gives a negative ΔG (forward is favored), Q > K gives a positive ΔG, and Q = K gives ΔG = 0.

mem: Q < K: runs forward, ΔG negative
Q > K: runs in reverse, ΔG positive
Q = K: equilibrium, ΔG = 0
ΔG = RT ln(Q/K)

fm.f: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K), where R = gas constant, T = temperature in kelvin, Q = reaction quotient, K = equilibrium constant
fm.v: R and T = positive numbers; Q < K, so Q/K < 1; sign of ΔG = ?
fm.why: It ties the current mixture to the direction the reaction will go.
fm.nc: You only need the sign of the log: ln of a number below 1 is negative, ln of 1 is 0, and ln of a number above 1 is positive.

steps: Write the formula: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K).
Write down the values: R and T are always positive; Q is less than K.
Since Q < K, the fraction Q/K is less than 1.
The natural log of a number less than 1 is negative, so ln(Q/K) < 0.
Multiply: ΔG = (positive) × (negative) = negative.
A negative ΔG means the forward reaction is favored, so it runs forward until Q = K.
d_5E_3.sc: Q smaller than K means too little product, so the reaction moves forward to make more.
d_5E_3.trap: Flipping the comparison. Q less than K means too much reactant, so the shift is forward.
d_5E_3.plain: If a pot has less soup than the recipe calls for, you keep cooking until you reach the right amount.

ox: Correct. Breaking a bond takes energy (endothermic), and forming a bond releases energy (exothermic). So a reaction's ΔH is roughly the energy of the bonds broken minus the energy of the bonds formed.

Not quite. Breaking a bond always costs energy. The idea that 'breaking releases energy' often comes from how people describe ATP. In reality the energy released comes from forming new, more stable bonds and interactions.
Not quite. When two atoms form a bond, they settle into a lower-energy, more stable arrangement, and the extra energy is released. Forming bonds gives off energy.
Not quite. Breaking bonds is endothermic, taking energy in. Only forming bonds is exothermic. They can't both release energy.

p: Bond energy is the energy needed to pull two bonded atoms apart. Because you have to add energy to do it, breaking a bond is endothermic, meaning it absorbs heat. When those atoms join back together, the same energy is released, so forming a bond is exothermic.
A reaction breaks some bonds and forms others. Its enthalpy change, ΔH, is roughly the energy you put in to break the old bonds minus the energy you get back from forming the new ones.
If the new bonds are stronger than the old ones, more energy comes out than goes in, and ΔH is negative (exothermic). If the old bonds were stronger, ΔH is positive.

mem: Break bonds: energy in (endothermic)
Form bonds: energy out (exothermic)
ΔH ≈ Σ broken − Σ formed
Stronger bonds formed than broken: ΔH negative
d_5E_9.trap: Thinking energy is released when a bond breaks.
d_5E_9.plain: Pulling two magnets apart takes effort. When they snap back together, they give that energy back with a click.

ox: Correct. A catalyst gives the reaction an easier path with a lower activation energy (the energy hill to start). It speeds forward and reverse equally, so ΔG and K do not change.
Wrong. A catalyst only gets you to equilibrium faster. It does not change where equilibrium sits, because K is unchanged.
Wrong. ΔG depends only on the start and end states (state function). A catalyst changes the path, not the endpoints.
Wrong. A catalyst is regenerated at the end of each cycle, so it is not used up. Students confuse it with a reactant.

p: A catalyst is a helper that makes a reaction faster by lowering activation energy, the energy hill reactants must climb. It does this by offering a different route.
The start and end energies stay the same, so ΔG, ΔH and K do not change. The catalyst is not used up. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

mem: Lowers Ea, speeds both directions equally
Does not change ΔG, ΔH or K
Not consumed
Does not shift equilibrium
q84.trap: Thinking a catalyst makes a reaction more favorable (more negative ΔG) or shifts it toward products.
q84.plain: A catalyst is a tunnel through a hill. You get to the other side faster, but the other side is still the same place.

ox: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH negative, and ΔS positive making -TΔS also negative, both terms are negative at any T. So ΔG is always negative.
Wrong. High T only is for ΔH positive and ΔS positive.
Wrong. Low T only is for ΔH negative and ΔS negative.
Wrong. Never spontaneous is ΔH positive and ΔS negative.

p: A reaction is spontaneous (goes on its own) if ΔG is negative. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is temperature in kelvin (always positive).
Negative ΔH means heat is released, which is favorable. Positive ΔS means more disorder, which is also favorable. Both help, so ΔG is negative at every temperature.

mem: -ΔH, +ΔS: always spontaneous
+ΔH, -ΔS: never spontaneous
Same signs: temperature decides

q85.plain: A ball rolling downhill that is also being pushed from behind will always roll.

ox: Correct. Halving the volume raises pressure. Le Chatelier's principle says the system relieves the stress by moving to the side with fewer gas moles. Left has 1 + 3 = 4 moles, right has 2 moles, so it shifts toward NH₃.
Wrong. The N₂ and H₂ side has more gas moles (4), so it would raise pressure further. This is the reverse of the correct shift.
Wrong. No shift happens only when both sides have equal gas moles. Here it is 4 versus 2.
Wrong. K changes only with temperature. Pressure or volume changes shift the position but not the value of K.

p: Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to partly undo the disturbance. Squeezing a gas mixture raises pressure.
The system lowers pressure by making fewer gas molecules. Count gas moles on each side and move toward the smaller number. K itself does not change.

mem: Volume down or pressure up: shift to fewer gas moles
Volume up: shift to more gas moles
Equal moles: no shift
Only temperature changes K

q86.trap: Thinking K changes when pressure or volume changes.
q86.plain: In a crowded room, if the room shrinks, people pair up to take less space.

ox: Wrong. First order means doubling [A] doubles the rate (2¹ = 2), not quadruples it.
Correct. Rate is proportional to [A]ⁿ. Doubling [A] multiplies rate by 2ⁿ. The rate rose 4 times, and 2² = 4, so n = 2.
Wrong. Zero order means rate does not depend on [A] (2⁰ = 1), so the rate would not change.
Wrong. Fourth order would give 2⁴ = 16 times the rate. The students confuse the factor 4 with the order.

p: Reaction order tells how rate depends on a concentration. In rate = k[A]ⁿ, n is the order, and k is the rate constant.
If you change [A] by a factor and the rate changes by another factor, then (concentration factor)ⁿ = (rate factor). Solve for n.

Double [A], rate x2: first order
Double [A], rate x4: second order

q87.trap: Picking 'fourth' because the rate changed by 4.
q87.plain: If doubling your pizza order makes the mess four times bigger, the mess grows by the square.

ox: Correct. In an endothermic reaction, heat is like a reactant. Adding heat (raising T) pushes the reaction toward products, so K increases.
Wrong. K decreases with higher T for exothermic reactions, where heat is a product. The trap is mixing up the two.
Wrong. K depends on temperature. It is the only common thing that changes K.
Wrong. Higher T speeds the rate, but it also changes K. 'Only rate' is wrong.

p: K is the equilibrium constant: the ratio of products to reactants when things stop changing. Temperature is the one thing that changes K.

Treat heat as a reactant or product. Endothermic (absorbs heat): heat is a reactant, so adding heat favors products and K goes up. Exothermic: heat is a product, so adding heat favors reactants and K goes down.

mem: Endothermic: T up, K up
Exothermic: T up, K down
Only T changes K

q88.trap: Applying the exothermic rule to an endothermic reaction.
q88.plain: If a recipe needs heat to work, a hotter oven makes more of the finished dish.

ox: Correct. A closed system lets energy, as heat or work, cross its boundary, but no matter gets in or out. A sealed flask you can heat is a good example: it warms up, but nothing escapes.
Not quite. An open system exchanges both matter and energy. Think of an open pot of boiling water: heat goes in, and steam (matter) escapes. The question rules out matter crossing.
Not quite. An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy. A perfect thermos is the idea. Since this system can exchange energy, it isn't isolated.
Not quite. Isothermal means the temperature stays constant during a process. It's a word about how a process happens, not a type of system or boundary.

p: In thermodynamics, the system is the part of the universe you're paying attention to, like the gas in a cylinder. The surroundings are everything else. The boundary is the dividing line between them.
Systems are named by what can cross that boundary. Open: matter and energy both cross. Closed: only energy crosses, as heat or work. Isolated: nothing crosses.
Words like isothermal (constant temperature), isobaric (constant pressure) and adiabatic (no heat flow) describe processes, not system types. Don't mix the two lists up.

mem: Open: matter and energy
Closed: energy only
Isolated: neither
Isothermal: constant temperature, a process word
x5E_004.trap: Picking isothermal because it sounds like thermodynamics. It isn't a boundary type.
x5E_004.plain: A sealed lunchbox on a sunny windowsill. Heat can get in and warm the food, but the food can't get out.

ox: Not quite. Elements in their standard states are assigned ΔH°f = 0. That's a bookkeeping choice for enthalpy, a starting line for measuring heat. Their entropy S° is still positive at 25 °C, because their atoms are moving and can be arranged many ways.
Correct. The third law says a perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K has exactly one possible arrangement, one microstate. Using S = k ln W with W = 1 gives S = k × ln 1 = k × 0 = 0.
Not quite. 0 °C is not absolute zero. Kelvin = °C + 273, so 0 °C = 273 K. At that temperature gas molecules are flying around in countless arrangements, so gases have large positive entropy.
Not quite. A liquid at its freezing point still has molecules sliding around past each other, so it has many possible arrangements. Its entropy is well above zero.

p: Entropy (S) measures how many ways the particles in a substance can be arranged while it looks the same from the outside. Each arrangement is a microstate. More microstates means more entropy. The formula is S = k ln W, where W is the number of microstates and k is Boltzmann's constant.
At 0 K (absolute zero), particles have the least motion possible. In a perfect crystal of a pure substance, every particle sits in its one spot, so W = 1 and S = k ln 1 = 0.

That gives entropy a true zero point, so substances have absolute entropies, and every real substance above 0 K has S > 0. Enthalpy has no true zero; that's why chemists set ΔH°f = 0 for elements by agreement.

mem: S = 0 only for a perfect crystal at 0 K
Anything above 0 K has S > 0
ΔH°f = 0 for standard-state elements is a separate idea
S = k ln W, W = number of microstates
x5E_005.trap: Mixing up the ΔH°f = 0 rule for elements with the entropy rule.
x5E_005.plain: A perfectly neat toy box where every toy has exactly one spot. There's only one way for it to be that tidy.

ox: Correct. Adiabatic means q = 0, so the first law becomes ΔU = w. The expanding gas pushes on its surroundings and does work, so w is negative and U drops. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so T drops too.

Not quite. No heat flowing in or out doesn't mean the temperature holds still. Work can change internal energy on its own, and here the gas spends energy doing work. Constant temperature would be an isothermal process, which is different.
Not quite. Taking up more room doesn't warm a gas. To expand, the gas has to push its surroundings back, and that costs it energy. With no heat coming in to make up for it, the gas cools.

Not quite. The heat capacity tells you how much the temperature changes for a given energy change, so it sets the size of the drop. But the direction is already decided: ΔU = w, and w is negative, so T has to go down.

concept.t: The first law and adiabatic expansion
p: The first law of thermodynamics is energy bookkeeping: ΔU = q + w. U is internal energy, the total energy of the particles. q is heat added to the system. w is work done on the system. (Some books flip the sign of w; the MCAT usually uses this one.)

Adiabatic means no heat crosses the boundary, so q = 0 and ΔU = w. When a gas expands, it pushes the surroundings away and does work on them, so w is negative and U falls. When a gas is compressed, the surroundings do work on it, so w is positive and U rises.
For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature. So adiabatic expansion cools the gas, and adiabatic compression heats it.

mem: Adiabatic: q = 0, so ΔU = w
Expanding gas: w < 0, so T falls
Compressed gas: w > 0, so T rises
Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0
x5E_007.sc: Adiabatic expansion cools; adiabatic compression heats.
x5E_007.trap: Thinking 'no heat exchange' means 'no temperature change.'
x5E_007.plain: Spray an aerosol can for a while and the can gets cold. The gas spends its own energy pushing its way out.

fig.cap: When heat q leaves a hot body and enters a cooler one, the cooler body gains more entropy (q/T) than the hot one loses, so ΔS(universe) > 0.

ox: Not quite. The system's own entropy can drop in a spontaneous process. Water freezing below 0 °C is an example: the water becomes more ordered, but the heat it releases raises the surroundings' entropy by more. The law is about the total.
Not quite. Lower enthalpy (giving off heat) helps, but it isn't required. Ice melting at room temperature absorbs heat (ΔH positive) and still happens on its own, because the entropy gain wins.
Correct. The second law says the entropy of the universe, system plus surroundings, increases in every spontaneous process. Written out: ΔS_universe > 0.
Not quite. The total energy of the universe stays constant. That's the first law, conservation of energy. Energy can change form, but the total never goes up or down.

p: Entropy (S) measures how spread out energy and matter are, or how many ways the particles can be arranged. The second law says that in any spontaneous process, one that happens on its own without outside help, the total entropy of the universe increases.

'Universe' means system plus surroundings. One part can lose entropy as long as the other part gains more. A refrigerator makes its inside colder and more ordered, but it dumps even more heat, and entropy, into your kitchen.
The first law is the energy rule (total energy stays constant). The second law is the entropy rule (total entropy goes up). Keep them straight.

mem: Spontaneous: ΔS_universe > 0
First law: total energy of the universe is constant
The system's entropy alone doesn't decide
x5E_008.trap: Applying the second law to the system alone instead of the whole universe.
x5E_008.plain: Tidying your room makes it less messy, but you burn energy and give off heat doing it. Count everything and the total mess in the world still goes up.

ox: Correct. A reversible process moves through a chain of equilibrium states and creates no new entropy. The system's entropy change is exactly matched by the opposite change in the surroundings, so ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings = 0.

Not quite. A positive ΔS_universe is the mark of real, irreversible processes, like heat flowing from hot to cold or a gas rushing into a vacuum. The idealized reversible case creates no extra entropy.
Not quite. The second law says ΔS_universe can never be negative. A negative value would mean a process running backward on its own, like a mixed drink un-mixing.

Not quite. ΔH/T is the system's entropy change for a reversible change at constant temperature and pressure, like melting ice at exactly 0 °C. It's not the universe's total, which for a reversible process is 0.

p: A reversible process is an ideal, super-slow change where the system is always just a tiny nudge away from equilibrium. You could run it backward and leave no trace on the system or the surroundings. Real processes are never perfectly reversible, but it's a useful limit.
Since nothing is wasted, no new entropy gets created. Any entropy the system gains, the surroundings lose, and the total for the universe is 0.
Real processes are irreversible and always increase the universe's entropy. So: reversible, ΔS_universe = 0; irreversible, ΔS_universe > 0; never less than 0.

mem: Reversible: ΔS_universe = 0
Irreversible (real, spontaneous): ΔS_universe > 0
ΔS_universe < 0: never happens
x5E_011.trap: Mixing up the system's ΔS, which can be anything, with the universe's ΔS.
x5E_011.plain: A ball rolling up and down a perfectly smooth track with no friction. Nothing is lost, so it could go back and forth forever.

ox: Not quite. Plenty of reactions are endothermic, with a positive ΔH, like melting ice. Hess's law works the same way for any sign, so the sign can't be the reason.
Not quite. Heat measured at constant volume equals ΔU, the change in internal energy. Heat at constant pressure is ΔH. Either way, this isn't what makes Hess's law work.

Correct. Enthalpy is a state function: ΔH depends only on the starting and ending states, not on the path. So any set of steps that adds up to the overall reaction gives the same total ΔH, and you can add the steps' ΔH values together.
Not quite. ΔH is extensive, meaning it scales with how much reacts: double the amounts, double the ΔH. That's true and you use it in Hess's law problems, but it's not why the law works.

p: A state function is a property that depends only on the current state of the system, not on how it got there. Enthalpy (H), internal energy (U), entropy (S) and Gibbs free energy (G) are all state functions. Heat (q) and work (w) are not; they depend on the path.

Since H is a state function, ΔH for going from reactants to products is the same no matter which route you take. Hess's law uses this: add up the ΔH values of steps that combine to the overall reaction.
Two bookkeeping rules: if you reverse a step, flip the sign of its ΔH. If you multiply a step by a number, multiply its ΔH by the same number.

Watch your signs. Most ΔH°f values are negative, so subtracting a negative reactant sum actually adds to the total.

concept.t: Why boiling takes more energy than melting
p: The enthalpy of fusion (ΔHfus) is the heat needed to melt 1 mole of a solid. The enthalpy of vaporization (ΔHvap) is the heat needed to turn 1 mole of liquid into gas. Both are spent overcoming intermolecular forces, which for water are mainly hydrogen bonds.

In a liquid, molecules are still touching and still attracted to each other; they just aren't locked in place. In a gas, they're far apart with almost no attraction left. So going from liquid to gas breaks far more attractions than going from solid to liquid.
For water, ΔHvap is about 41 kJ/mol and ΔHfus is about 6 kJ/mol. The same pattern holds for basically every substance: ΔHvap is much bigger than ΔHfus.

concept.t: Entropy change during a phase change
p: Entropy (S) measures how spread out energy and particles are. When a substance melts or boils at its transition temperature, heat goes in but the temperature doesn't change; the energy goes into loosening the attractions between molecules.
At that temperature the change is reversible, so ΔS = q_rev ÷ T. The heat absorbed is just the enthalpy of the phase change, ΔH. T must be in kelvin, and ΔH must be in J if you want ΔS in J/(mol·K).
Melting and boiling always have positive ΔS, because liquids are more disordered than solids and gases far more than liquids. Freezing and condensing have negative ΔS.

Not quite. A cooling block has less thermal energy and its particles move less, so its entropy goes down. The question says so directly. The process is still spontaneous because the room gains more.

concept.t: Why heat flows from hot to cold
p: The second law says a process is spontaneous when the total entropy of the system plus surroundings increases. One part can lose entropy as long as the other part gains more.

When heat q moves at temperature T, the entropy change is about q ÷ T. The same amount of heat makes a bigger entropy difference at a low temperature than at a high one, because you're dividing by a smaller number.

So when heat leaves something hot and enters something cold, the cold side gains more entropy than the hot side loses. That's why heat flows from hot to cold on its own, and never the other way without outside work.

concept.t: How temperature tips the balance in ΔG
p: Gibbs free energy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, tells you whether a process is favored at a given temperature. Negative ΔG means it goes on its own; positive means the reverse is favored.

When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature decides. Here both are negative: the heat given off helps, but the loss of freedom hurts, and the hurt gets bigger as T rises because it's multiplied by T. So folding wins at low temperature and unfolding wins at high temperature.
The crossover is where ΔG = 0. Rearranging 0 = ΔH − TΔS gives T = ΔH ÷ ΔS. Put ΔH and ΔS in the same energy unit (J) first.

ΔH negative and ΔS negative: favored at low T

Not quite. A negative ΔG means the process releases free energy, which is exactly what can be harnessed as useful work. A process with ΔG = 0 is the one that can't do any.

concept.t: Free energy is the energy you can use
p: Gibbs free energy (G) is the part of a system's energy that's available to do useful work at constant temperature and pressure. 'Useful' work, also called non-expansion work, means work other than a gas pushing against outside pressure: muscle contraction, building ATP, pumping ions, running a battery.
The most useful work you can get from a process is −ΔG. That maximum is reached only in an ideal, reversible process. Real processes always get less, because some energy leaks out as heat.
This is why biochemists care so much about ΔG: a reaction with ΔG = −50 kJ/mol can power, at most, another process that needs 50 kJ/mol.

concept.t: Calorimetry: heat lost equals heat gained
p: Specific heat (c) is how much heat it takes to warm 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C. Water's is high, about 4.2 J/(g·°C); most metals are much lower. The heat moved is q = mcΔT.

When a hot object and a cold one are mixed in an insulated container, no heat escapes. So the heat lost by the hot one equals the heat gained by the cold one, and both end at the same final temperature.

Each object's ΔT runs from its own starting temperature to the shared final temperature. A small specific heat means a big temperature change for the same heat, which is why the metal dropped 60 °C while the water rose only 5 °C.

Gas to solid is deposition; solid to gas is sublimation. Dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimes at normal room pressure because 1 atm is below CO₂'s triple-point pressure.

concept.t: Finding a rate law from initial rates
p: A rate law tells you how the reaction speed depends on each concentration: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. The exponents m and n are the orders, and you can't read them off the balanced equation; they come from experiments.

When two concentrations change at once, their effects multiply. So you can divide out the one you already know to find the other.

concept.t: How half-life depends on reaction order
p: Half-life is the time for a reactant's concentration to drop to half its starting value. Whether it stays the same or changes depends on the reaction order.

In a zero-order reaction, the rate doesn't depend on [A] at all, so the same amount disappears every second. Removing half of a smaller pile takes less time, so each half-life is shorter: t½ = [A]₀ ÷ (2k).

In a first-order reaction, the half-life is constant: t½ = 0.693 ÷ k. That's why radioactive decay, which is first order, has a fixed half-life. In a second-order reaction, t½ = 1 ÷ (k[A]₀), so each half-life gets longer.

ox: Not quite. A product-like transition state belongs to a strongly endothermic step, where the products are high in energy and close to the peak. This choice reverses the early/late rule.
Not quite. A transition state is an energy peak, not an intermediate sitting in a valley. And in a highly exothermic step the peak isn't halfway along; it comes early, near the reactants.
Not quite. The whole point of the Hammond postulate is that structure follows energy: species that are close in energy look alike. So energy does tell you something about structure.

Correct. In a highly exothermic step, the products are far lower in energy than the reactants, so the peak sits close in energy to the reactants. By the Hammond postulate, it's an early transition state that looks a lot like the reactants.

p: Every reaction step has a transition state: the arrangement of atoms at the very top of the energy hill, with bonds half broken and half formed. You can't isolate it, but you can reason about what it looks like.
The Hammond postulate says the transition state resembles whichever species is closer to it in energy. Species close in energy tend to be close in structure.

For a strongly exothermic (downhill) step, the peak is near the reactants in energy, so the transition state is early and reactant-like. For a strongly endothermic (uphill) step, the peak is near the products, so it's late and product-like.

mem: Exothermic step: early transition state, looks like reactants
Endothermic step: late transition state, looks like products
Close in energy means close in structure

Correct. Reversing the reaction turns K = 4.0 into 1 ÷ 4.0 = 0.25. Doubling every coefficient squares it: 0.25² = (1/4)² = 1/16 = 0.0625.

Not quite. 0.125 is (1/4) × (1/2) = 1/8. That treats doubling the coefficients as multiplying K by 2 (or ½). But doubling the coefficients raises K to the power of 2; it squares K rather than multiplying it.

p: K is products over reactants, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. For A ⇌ 2B, K = [B]² ÷ [A].
If you reverse the reaction, products and reactants swap places, so the new K is 1/K. If you multiply every coefficient by n, every exponent gets multiplied by n, so the new K is Kⁿ.
If both happen, do both: flip, then raise to the power. And if you add two reactions together, multiply their K values.

Multiply coefficients by n: K becomes Kⁿ

Write down the values: K = 4.0. Doubling A ⇌ 2B gives 2A ⇌ 4B, so n = 2, and 4B ⇌ 2A is that written backward.
Square for the doubled coefficients: (1/4)² = 1² ÷ 4² = 1 ÷ 16.

ox: Not quite. The total pressure does go up, which makes this tempting. But equilibrium depends on the partial pressure of each reacting gas, and argon isn't part of the expression. Those partial pressures haven't changed, so Le Chatelier's 'more pressure, fewer moles' rule doesn't kick in.
Not quite. A shift toward products would need Q to drop below K. Adding argon doesn't change any of the reacting gases' amounts, so Q stays the same and there's no push either way.
Not quite. K depends only on temperature. Adding an inert gas, or changing amounts, volume or pressure, never changes K.
Correct. The container's volume is fixed, so each reacting gas keeps the same moles in the same space. Its partial pressure (and concentration) is unchanged, so Q still equals K, and nothing shifts.

concept.t: Adding an inert gas to an equilibrium
p: An equilibrium shifts only when something makes Q (the reaction quotient) different from K. Q is built from the partial pressures or concentrations of the gases that actually take part in the reaction.

An inert gas, like argon, doesn't react. At constant volume, adding it raises the total pressure, but each reacting gas still has the same moles in the same volume. Their partial pressures don't change, Q stays equal to K, and there's no shift.

It's different at constant total pressure. Then adding argon makes the container expand, each reacting gas gets more spread out, and the reaction shifts toward the side with more moles of gas. Only temperature changes K itself.

mem: Inert gas, constant volume: no shift
Inert gas, constant pressure: shift toward more gas moles
Only temperature changes K

Correct. With reversible steps and enough heat and time, the mixture reaches equilibrium. At equilibrium, the more stable product wins. P2 has the more negative ΔG° (−40 vs. −10 kJ/mol), so it dominates. This is called thermodynamic control.
Not quite. Both pathways being open doesn't mean you get equal amounts. At equilibrium, the amounts depend on how stable each product is, and P2 is much more stable than P1.
Not quite. Both ΔG° values are negative, which means both products are lower in free energy than the reactant. So the reaction favors products, not reverting all the way back.

p: When a reaction can make two different products, two things can decide the winner. The kinetic product forms fastest because its activation energy (Eₐ) is lowest. The thermodynamic product is the most stable, with the most negative ΔG°.
If conditions are cold, short or the reaction can't run backward, products are locked in as they form, so the faster one wins. That's kinetic control.
If conditions are hot, long and reversible, products keep reverting and re-forming until the mixture reaches equilibrium. Then the most stable product wins. That's thermodynamic control.

mem: Kinetic product: lowest Eₐ, wins when cold, short or irreversible
Thermodynamic product: lowest G, wins when hot, long and reversible
At equilibrium, ΔG° decides, not Eₐ

ox: Not quite. The roles are backward. The product that wins in the cold is the one that forms fastest, so the 1,2-adduct is the fast (kinetic) one. The product that wins when things can equilibrate is the stable one, so the 1,4-adduct is the more stable (thermodynamic) one.

Correct. At −80 °C the addition is effectively one-way, so the fastest-forming product, the 1,2-adduct, wins. At 40 °C the adducts can revert and interconvert, so the more stable 1,4-adduct, with its more substituted double bond, takes over.
Not quite. If both adducts were equally stable, letting them equilibrate at 40 °C wouldn't favor the 1,4-adduct. The fact that it takes over when warm tells you it's more stable.

Not quite. Warming doesn't change which path has the lower barrier or which product is more stable. What changes is that at higher temperature the products have enough energy to revert, so the mixture can settle to equilibrium.

p: When HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene, H⁺ adds first and makes a carbocation (a positively charged carbon) whose charge is shared over two carbons by resonance. Br⁻ can attack either one, giving the 1,2-adduct or the 1,4-adduct.
The 1,2-adduct forms faster, partly because Br⁻ is still right next to that carbon. So at low temperature, when products can't turn back, the 1,2-adduct dominates: kinetic control.

The 1,4-adduct has its C=C in the middle of the chain, with more carbons attached, and more substituted double bonds are more stable. At higher temperature the products can revert and re-form, so the mixture settles toward the 1,4-adduct: thermodynamic control.

mem: Low temperature: kinetic product (1,2 for HBr + butadiene)
Higher temperature: thermodynamic product (1,4)
More substituted double bond: more stable
